Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege in connection with an editorial in the Montreal Gazette of Saturday, April 6, entitled Regarding Misrepresentation. I will only-read a few lines from the editorial which I think will be sufficient to indicate the point I intend to deal with. They are as follows:
Nor is the Peace River member any more fortunate in his denial of the statement that, from one of the divisions of the session of 1926, the government emerged with a majority of one, including, his vote. "There never was such a division in that session," he says.
After omitting a few lines, the editorial continues:
Mr. Kennedy attempts to set up a case by referring to the votes cast by him in the "hectic divisions" immediately preceding the dissolution, but those were not the only divisions of the session, nor were they the only "hectic" ones. The government was on the edge of disaster from the very opening day of the session, and while nearly every division was critical, some were much more so than others. There was, for example, the vote on February 2, on Mr. Stansell's motion to adjourn the debate on the customs inquiry, a vital issue then, as later. Perhaps Mr. Kennedy will say that this was not a hectic vote; it is' a matter which we will have to take up with the government which, at the time, regarded the Stansell motion as of such importance as to force a division. A vote was taken, and the Stansell motion was defeated by 119 to 118, and if Mr. Kennedy will look at the Hansard of that year and month and day he will find among the 119 nays the name "Kennedy (Peace River)."
The vote referred to took place on February 2, 1926, and my statement that there had not been such a division came immediately after quoting an article in the Montreal Gazette of March 5, 1928, which read as follows:
But he-

Sometimes a member raises as a question of privilege what is, at most, merely a question of order. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was on
the first of March that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) brought into the house the budget which we have now before us. It is just a month and two days since the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), in his dual capacity at the time of acting leader and financial critic of the opposition, undertook to reply at some length and to deliver a speech on behalf of the opposition in reference to the several matters in the budget and referred to in the speech of the Minister of Finance. From that time to the present, with the exception of the recess which we had at Easter and two days when another matter was precipitated into the discussion here, the house has continuously debated the budget, and it might appear that at this late stage of the debate little is left which has not already been said. May I say at once that my purpose in participating at this time is not so much in the expectation of contributing any new arguments, but rather for the sake of emphasizing the truth

of some of the representations which have been made on this side of the house, more particularly in reference to the speech by the hon. member for South Wellington.
It was perhaps natural that the speech of the hon. member for South Wellington should attract considerable attention at the time it was delivered, and also occasion much discussion in the course of the debate. My hon. friend took full advantage of his opportunity as acting leader of the opposition to speak at . length, and to cover, in so far as they relate to the finances of the country, the many subjects which were likely to be of interest in political discussion during the next year or two. My hon. friend has already been congratulated upon his speech on that occasion. He is an old parliamentarian; with the exception of yourself, Mr. Speaker, and the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), he is perhaps the oldest member in the house, certainly the oldest member sitting on the opposite side-. He has had great experience as a parliamentarian, and- also in his chosen profession, and he turned both to the best of advantage in the presentation of the statement which he made to parliament at that time. I should like to congratulate him on the manner of the presentation of his remarks on that occasion; I wish I could do likewise with respect to the substance of them. He congratulated the Minister of Finance on the lucidity of his speech, on its precision, on its conciseness, but I must say to my hon. friend that what his own address gained in lucidity it seemed to me to lack in accuracy. What it had of precision was in large part, to my mind, mere pretence, and if he was concise in many of his statements, he was, I regret to say, not wholly candid. That is the criticism which I have to bring against my hon. friend's remarks, a criticism which I shall endeavour to substantiate in what I have to say this afternoon.
There was, however, one remark made by my hon. friend to which I think no exception will be taken, certainly no exception on this side of the house, a remark which will be remembered long after much of the rest of his presentation will have been completely forgotten. He referred to the present as a time of prosperity, and he did not stop at the word prosperity, but he said, a time of unbounded prosperity. While my hon. friend has stated what I think the country as a whole recognizes to be the fact, he endeavoured strenuously to discover ways in which credit for this prosperity might be given in some quarter other than that of the
13S3

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
present administration. He spoke naturally of Providence and of the energy and ingenuity of the people of our country. Of this the Minister of Finance himself had I think already made full acknowledgment. He went on to say that it would be interesting for those on his side to speculate how much more prosperous the country would have been, and how much more general the prosperity, had another government been seated on this side. May I say to my hon. friend that if he is free to speculate in that way, we are similarly free to speculate and I think we may fairly say that if hon. gentlemen opposite had been in office, there is no doubt that the prosperity of the country would not have been what it is at the present time.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that this prosperity, far from being, as my hon. friend sought to infer, restricted and not distributed as between the different classes of the country, has been very general and has been shared in some measure by all classes throughout the country. It is a prosperity discoverable, first of all, with respect to the great basic industries of the country, on which the rest of our industrial development so largely depends. It is a prosperity which has been apparent in the manufacturing industries of the country, a prosperity which has been great with respect to the trade of the country, a prosperity which has manifested itself in increase of employment and in diminution oif unemployment, a prosperity that has shown itself in the activities of business and of banks and financial institutions, a prosperity which has also been disclosed in the savings of the people, and in their investments with respect to many matters which have to do with their standard of living.
It might be well, Mr. Speaker, in confirmation of what I have just said to give a few facts with respect to the present prosperity which will serve to indicate how general and how considerable that prosperity is. Before so doing, however, may I draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that the prosperity of the present year succeeds the prosperity of the year previous, which was noteworthy in the same particular; that, as a matter of fact, from the moment at which the government had found it possible to balance the public accounts there has been continual improvement in the public finances of the country, with which has come continuous prosperity until within the past year we have had a period of prosperity unmistakable in the history of Canada.
To begin with the basic industries, may I mention these facts with respect to agriculture, Canada's greatest basic industry?
78594-88J
T.he acreage under crop this past year, 1928, was 59,410,000 or 3,238,000 more than in 1927. The new land brought under crop this year represents an area half as large as the crop acreage of Manitoba

this on the top of continuous increases for many years past.
The wheat yield totalled over 533,000,000 bushels, or 53,000,000' greater than the previous high yield, or 14*5,000 000 greater than the average of the five years 192281926.
Exports of wheat reached the highest point ever recorded in a single month in November, 1928, namely, 75,416,000 bushels. The exports of 1928 were the highest ever recorded in a calendar year, namely, 365,428,561 bushels, valued at $433,767,578.
The previous largest twelve months was the year ending September, 1924, when the totals were only 294,000,000 bushels, valued at $302,000,000.
In mining we had the most active year in the history of Canada. The total value of production was $273,000,000, an increase of $24,000,000 over the total for 1927, the previous high year.
The chief activity was in copper, lead, zinc and nickel, but coal and gypsum made new high records, as did structural materials in general. Gold production was up, and cadmium, produced at Trail during 1928, was a newcomer among Canada's mineral products
Employment was about 7 per cent more active than 1927.
In forest products, newsprint production reached 2,382.011 tons in 1928, the highest on record, the previous peak being 2,086,949 in
1927.	Seven years ago, in 1921, the production was 805.000 tons.
Conditions in the fishing industry in 1928 were notably better than in 1927. With the possible exception of 1926, last year was the most successful experienced by Canadian fishermen since the Fordney tariff was made effective by the United States in 1922. The production had a marketed value of more than $54,000,000, or $11,500,000, in round figures, above the marketed value of the catch of 1923. The total catch of all fish was approximately
1.300,000,000 pounds.
One of the most significant features of 1928 was the fact that power installation work valued at over $300,000,000 was under way. When it is remembered that every dollar spent on primary power presupposes an expenditure of $5 or $6 on subsidiary industrial plant, it is apparent that we are in the midst of a process of adding something like $2,000,000,000 to the capital industrial plant of the Dominion.
With respect to manufactures, it is conservative to say that the gross value of manufactures in 1928 will exceed $3,500,000,000.

Coming next to trade, the figures show that with respect to foreign trade the exports of Canadian products for 1928 totalled $1,349,-

This is probably the highest favourable trade balance per [DOT]capita in the world. This favourable trade balance was achieved in spite of falling prices of wheat and newsprint, Canada's two leading exports; it is accordingly indicative of "real" trading volume. The physical volume of Canada's trade in 1928 was undoubtedly the largest on record. Our total trade at 1918-20 prices would have run to at least 3J billions of dolUrs.

The huge proportions which the tourist trade has now attained is worthy of special mention under the heading of domestic trade. In 1927 it amounted to $242,754,000, and the estimate for the year just passed is substantially higher.
Coming now to transportation, carloadings totaled 3,697,106 cars in 1928, compared with 3,398,797 cars in 1927, an increase of 9 per cent, notwithstanding the diversion to motor trucking in progress.
The gross earnings of the Canadian National lines and of tihe Canadian Pacific Railway for 1928 were approximately 507.400,000, as against 450.000,000 in 1927.
The Canadian National system (including lines in the United States) had gross revenues of approximately $276,600,000, and net revenues of $53,200,000

all new high records.
The St, Lawrence canal traffic was the heaviest on record-almost half a million tons higher than last year, the previous high record. The Welland also made a new record.
With regard to labour, the general index of all employment was 111.6 in 1928, as compared with 104.6 in 1927, or an increase of 6.7 per cent.
The year was comparatively free from serious industrial disturbances. The time loss through strikes during the past three years was lower than at any time since 1915.
Let me refer to public finances and private savings and investments. The total ordinary revenues of the Dominion including special receipts and credits on consolidated fund, have reached $439,413,000 in the calendar year 1928, an increase of $30,214,000 notwithstanding the substantial reductions in the tariff of the last budget. This has enabled $53,000,000 of the national debt to be paid off, representing a saving of $2,650,000 in annual interest charges.
In banking, the savings deposits of banks increased from. $1,431,000,000 on November 30,
1927,	to $1,523500,000 on tihe same date of last year. Never before 1928 have saving deposits reached $1,500 millions.
Current loans, reflecting the strong demand for credit in connection with commercial and speculative transactions have shown an even greater increase than notice deposits. Such loans on November 30 last amounted to $1,238,000,000, an increase of $158,600,000 over the same date of 1927.
The sales of ordinary life insurance based on reports of fifteen companies having in force 84 per cent of the outstanding ordinary insurance in Canada, were $580,674,000 in
1928,	compared with $502,000,000 in 1927, an increase of more than 15 per cent.

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
The year may be summed up as follows:-
Unprecedentedly heavy production, earnings and profits in agriculture and all the other basic industries and occupations of the people.
Based on this, a heavy investment of savings, not only in existing enterprises but in the launching of new enterprises on an unprecedented scale-a process which has attracted foreign as well as Canadian capital.
An especially gratifying feature as I have already said, is that the prevailing prosperity is well distributed over the various provinces; it is as general for the different economic areas as it is for the different economic classes represented in the Dominion.
I have taken the trouble, Mr. Speaker, to make these facts a matter of record in Hansard, first of all, because they reflect a condition in the country of which, I think, we have all great, reason to be proud, but also because they will serve, as I speak a little later on. to answer some of the points which my hon. friend made in the course of his remarks, with respect to the burden of taxation and the ability to pay. Strive as mjr hon. friend and his associates may not to credit- the government with aught on account of this prosperity, they will have difficulty in having the country believe that the policies which we have put in force during the last seven years have not been in large part responsible for the progress which I have just mentioned.
The existing prosperity is due in no small measure to the fact- that we have restored confidence in the public finances of the country. When we came into office, for years preceding there had been deficits upon deficits in the public accounts. Those deficits have been changed into surpluses under the present administration. When we came into office, what are to-day the Canadian National railways, a splendidly organized system, were an aggregation of bankrupt roads in the nature of liabilities to the country; to-day they are looked upon as one of the country's greatest assets. The hon. Minister of Finance in his endeavour to encourage production and to bring relief to the farming community of this country, in one of his outstanding budgets introduced early after coming into office, reduced the duties on the implements of production in all the basic industries, mining, lumbering, fishing and agriculture, with a view to making the cost of production less in these great basic industries. The prosperity which we have to-day is in part a reflection of the budgets of my hon. friend in that particular. Similarly, the hon. Minister of Railways and
Canals (Mr. Dunning) has brought in measures in connection with the railways of this country, providing for increased branch lines, which have had the effect of opening up new districts and so helping to bring about the prosperity of which we are now justly proud. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) as the house well knows, has been energetic in expanding the trade facilities of his department, increasing the representation of his commercial agents abroad, and, along with the Minister of Finance, has helped to further treaties than have been of great service in the expansion of our trade. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) has brought in many measures which have been of distinct advantage to the farming community and of advantage as well in the marketing abroad of the products of this country. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan), has made a record for the country and for himself in the promotion and maintenance of industrial' peace.
I might say also, Mr. Speaker, with respect to the government's policies in other directions, that we have through pursuing a policy of goodwill towards all parts of the British Empire and towards other countries, done much to- further friendly relations between this country and the countries most closely associated with us, and in so doing have helped to forward the general -prosperity of Canada. The establishment of legations in the United States, Prance and Japan, are a part of that policy c-f international goodwill. Despite, therefore what my hon. friend has said, the country. I feel sure, will conclude that a prosperity which is unsurpassed in the history of Canada owes not a little to an administration in which fortunately the country itself has confidence at the present time.
May I come now more particularly to some of the financial matters mentioned by my hon. friend from South Wellington. He first of all undertook to deal with the debt of the country. He well knows, the house knows and the country knows that under the present administration the public debt of Canada has been very considerably reduced; indeed, it is one of the great achievements of the administration that the reduction in the public debt has been what it is. My hon. friend could not deny the reduction in the public debt, but he sought to lead the country to -believe that the reduction had been very much less than it actually has been. My hon. friend said that the only debt we should take any account of is the funded debt. In Great Britain, he said, they do not take

speechtext:

In making a comparison between the two periods, it should be borne in mind that in speaking of revenues and taxation the hon. gentleman opposite did not take into account
any payments for war expenses, while we are obliged to take into account, and dc take into account, in addition to present expenditures due to the war and which constitute 47 per cent of the whole, the amounts by which we are reducing the public debt, which reduction is really in the nature ot making payment on the cost of the war. ^ In other words, it has been left to the administrations which succeeded hon. gentlemen opposite not only to meet payments subsequently arising out of the war, but to meet the whole cost of the war, an.d in addition to meet the interest payments on the sums which were paid out during the period of the war. I think it is true to State that, 42 cents out of every dollar spent by the present administration is in one way or another an expenditure on account of the war.
My hon. friend mentioned a sinking fund and said that he thought the Minister of Finance should establish such a fund. One of his reasons for advocating a sinking fund was that the temptation to spend too much money might be reproved from the Minister of Finance. If the minister were not presenting to the house the surpluses which he has, were he not reducing the public debt at the rate he is reducing it-$69,000,000 this year-there might be something in the argument for the immediate institution of a sinking fund to ensure that a given amount would be paid every year. If the hon. gentlemen opposite were in office I should say it would be eminently desirable to have a sinking fund. They did the financing of this country during their term of office by borrowing while we are meeting our obligations out of taxation. We are meeting our obligations and at the same time reducing in a very substantial way the public debt, At the same time, I agree with my hon. friend as to the value ordinarily of a sinking fund. I believe it is a desirable institution and I hope that one of these days a sinking fund will be made a part of our scheme of finance.
The next subject to which my hon friend referred was the rate of taxation and the burden of taxation. In the course of his remarks the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) said:
But who cares about the rate of taxation? The rate does not count. The only thing that counts in this world in regard to taxes is the burden of taxation-the load which the people have to carry. If my hon. friend would read tile speeches of the late William Ewart Gladstone, when he was Chancellor of the Exchequer in England, on this very point he would get some light. Gladstone pointed out very definitely that the rate of taxation means nothing; the burden of taxation means everything.

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
Who cares about the rate? Everyone cares, and no one more than my hon. friend himself. When he speaks about Mr. Gladstone's references to the rate and to the burden of taxation he overlooks the fact that Mr. Gladstone never spoke of the burden in contrast to the rate; he spoke of the burden in relation to the adjustment of burdens and in this regard he attached all importance to the rate. He said that the saime rate meant an injustice so far as the different classes were concerned. He was continually emphasizing that fact, and especially so in his great speech on the income tax in 1850. At that time he stressed, above everything else, the injustice of an income tax which fixed one rate for all classes in the community, because all classes were not equally in a position to bear the burden.
My hon. friend knows that there is an all-important factor in considering the burden of taxation, and that is the ability to pay. That is an all-important consideration. A 10 per cent tax on a man who has an income of
81,000	would be a very considerable burden; it means $100 taken out of $1,000, $900 are left after the tax is paid. A 10 per cent tax on a. man who has an income of $10,000 amounts to $1,000, and it is relatively not so hard a burden to bear, $9,000 are left after the tax is paid. W hen a man has to pay on an income of $100,000 it about reaches the point where he does not feel a 10 per cent tax as a burden ait all. In the light of figures which I have already given to the house I think it must be fully apparent that the ability to pay has -become -increasingly greater so far as all classes of society in t-his country are concerned.
Mr. Gladstone's views with respect to the burden and the rate of taxation may be gauged from the following passage which ippears on page 56, volume 2, of Morley's Life of Gladstone:
It has often been said that he ignored the ?ocial question; did not even seem to know there was one. The truth is, that what marks inm trom other chancellors is exactly the dom-mating hold gamed by the social question in all its depth and_ breadth upon his most susceptible imagination. Tariff reform, adjustment of burdens, invincible repugnance to waste or prolusion, accurate keeping and continuous scrutiny ot accounts, substitution of a few good taxes tor many bad ones,-all these were not merely the love of a methodical and thrifty man for nabits ot business; they were directly associated m him with the amelioration of the hard lot of the toiling mass, and sprang from an ardent concern m improving human well-being, and raising the moral ideals of mankind.
Elsewhere, at page 471, volume 1, of his Life of Gladstone, referring to Gladstone's examination of the income tax, Morley says Gladstone spoke of " the sense in the public mind 'Mr. Mackenzie King.]
of its injustice in laying the same rate upon the holder of idle and secured public funds, upon the industrious trader, upon the precarious earnings of the professional man."
I would say to my hon. friend that the course pursued by Mr. Gladstone is exactly the line on which the present administration has been proceeding in the matter of its tax reforms; we have been seeking to ameliorate the lot of those who are less fortunate. We have followed this course with respect to our reductions in the -tariff and in our treatment of tire income tax, in .the reduction of the sales tax, the rate of postage and other measures. We have attempted to follow .precisely the line of policy which Mr. Gladstone, perhaps the greatest of all chancellors of the exchequer, laid down in his day as the best procedure. May I say to my hon. friend that the one real criticism I have to make of him is this: He seems to have forsaken too largely his old leaders and his old principles. He did not learn about Mr. Gladstone in the school in which he is at the present time, but long ago, and he would be much better employed to-da.v were he to follow his old convictions and apply the principles he knows to be the right ones in the way in which Mir. Gladstone, amongst others, would have sought to have had them applied.
I come to the next subject dealt with by my hon. friend. He treated next of the cost of government and undertook to say that the cost of government had been increased considerably since the present administration had taken office. He referred more particularly to the last four years. If my hon. friend looks over the figures for the last four years in connection with the increased cost of government as it is disclosed by the records, he will find that it comes to something like 10 per cent during this period of great prosperity. I will not trouble quoting the remarks of my hon. friend, but I make that general statement which, I think, he will admit is correct. The figures are as follows:

I do not know what standard my hon. friend had before him in estimating the business of the country, but I have been trying to get together a few indices of the

business of the country-it is not an easy thing to gauge, but one can gauge it in a general way-to see whether the business of the country has not increased much more rapidly than any cost of government has increased, also to show whether the burden of taxation is not more easily borne than it was a few years ago, and whether the ability to pay on the part of the taxpayers is not greater than it has been at any time hitherto.
I give my hon. friend and the house the following figures which will help to illustrate something of the increased growth of business in Canada. These figures can, I believe, be substantiated.
It is estimated by statisticians pretty generally that the national wealth of Canada increased from S22,195,000,000 in 1922 to $26,691,000,000 in 1926, an increase in that period of 20 per cent. I admit it must take some collecting of data to reach the conclusion, but nevertheless that is what I believe those who speak with authority would quote.
The bank debits of chartered banks in 1924 totalled $27,157,000,000, while in 1928 they totalled $43,477,000,000, an increase of 60 per cent in these four years.
Life insurance in 1921 totalled $2,935,000,000, while in 1928 it is estimated that it totalled $5,609,000,000, an increase of 90 per cent.
As regards savings deposits in chartered banks, which are an indication of the position of individuals in the community, they increased from $1,197,000,000 in 1923, to $1,496,000.000 in 1928, an increase of 25 per cent.
Exports of Canadian products increased from $740,000,000 in 1922 to $1,356,000,000 in the last twelve months, or an increase of 80 per cent.
Gross revenue from all industries, according to the Financial Post of January 4, 1929, was in 1926, $6,188,000,000 and in 1928, $6,840,000,000, or an increase of 10 per cent in those two years.
The developed water-power of the country in 1921 was 2,700.000 horse-power and in 1928 it was 5,350.000 horse-power, or an increase of almost 100 per cent.
Motor vehicles increased from 465,000 in 1921, to 945,000 in 1927, or an increase of about 100 per cent.
The number of employees in the leading industrial establishments has increased by something like 20 per cent.
These are indices which, I think, should help anyone to arrive accurately at the improvement there has been in the business of the country in the last few years in comparison with the increase in the cost of government.
But if we wish to make a comparison of the cost of government that no one will question, let us make it between 1914 and the present time. This will help to disclose as between political parties how much the cost of government has increased, how much it has increased under the present Liberal administration in comparison with what it was before the war in the days of the Conservative administration. In that comparison I think the house will agree that it would be proper to exclude amounts which to-day we are paying on war account, such as pensions and the like, and which do not appear in the accounts of the year 1914. If we exclude these amounts, it will be found that the total expenditure of Canada to-day is very nearly the same as it was in 1914. If we go a step further and regard the receipts of the Post Office Department as payments for services rather than as a tax, and exclude, in addition to the expenses now being met on war account, the amounts of the Post Office department, a comparison of 1914 with the present day will show that the cost of government today is less than it was in 1914, and that, notwithstanding the great increase in the population of the country from 1914 to the present time, and notwithstanding the fact that the value of the dollar to-day is only two-thirds of what it was in 1914. I should like to place the exact figures on record because I think they are important for purposes of comparison.

My hon. friend undertook to deal with taxation. I stress this because I notice that hon. gentlemen opposite following him have continued to do the same. Let us compare, he said, the figures in consolidated revenue during the six years during which the Conservatives were in office, the period from 1918 to 1922, with the amount of total taxation during the period when the Liberal administration was in office. He then set out both sets of figures side by side and came to the conclusion that there was an annual increase in taxation under the present administration of $51,000,000. In other words, my hon. friend tried to have this house ana the country believe that under the present administration taxation, and meaning by taxation, the amount necessary to carry on the government, is $51,000,000 a year greater than is was during the years hon. gentlemen opposite were in office, and in presenting this plausible statement, he produced government accounts to show the total amounts paid into the consolidated revenue. They were very careful to see, while they were conscripting men for overseas service, that they did not conscript any of the wealth of the wealthy men of the country. They took good care to see that the bonds were issued at a very good price, that they carried a rate of interest of 5| per cent for those in a position to invest their wealth and that these persons would be secured in their privileged position by the government undertaking that these bonds would not be taxed at any time in the future. They could be stowed away among the assets of the well-to-do of the country by those who were fortunate enough to be able to purchase them, and the government of to-day in its efforts to raise taxation is, as a consequence, prevented from getting a dollar of the income derived from those bonds at the present time. Not only are we expected to make good the borrowings of my hon. friends opposite, but in this effort we are deprived of the very source of revenue which ought to be the first source from which it should be possible for a government to collect.

What was the result of this policy of borrowing rather than taxing? The annual interest bills of the Dominion increased 'by leaps and bounds. Whereas in the fiscal year ended 1917 the total interest payments of the Dominion of Canada were $35,802,000, they rose in the fiscal year ended 1918 to $47,845,000; 1919 to $77,431,000; 1920 to $107,527,000; 1921 to $139.551,000; falling somewhat in 1922 to $135,247,849.
In these five years the previous administration increased the interest bills of the people of Canada by no less than 100 millions a year. Owing to the rapidly increasing interest burdens resulting from the policy of wholesale borrowing instead of taxing during the war period, additional taxation had to be imposed, after the war to take care of the increased interest charges as well as pension obligations.
May I say that the only fair comparison between the two periods is to estimate how much in each case it would have taken to balance the budget. That is the only fair basis of comparison, and to see then what was left. If we take the period to which my hon. friend has referred, we will find that year after year, far from balancing the budget, there were these huge deficits, all of which at a later period had to be met by taxation. Yes, in 1919. He goes on to say:
The leader of the government (Mr. Mackenzie King) was not, I think, in the house until September of the year 1919, when he was returned for a constituency in Prince Edward Island and came back to the house as leader of the Liberal party. But he was present in the house during the session of 1919 and I recall with the greatest distinctness what transpired during that session. So will my right hon. friend; so will the Minister of Finance; so would the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) if he were in his place.
Well, he is here now.
A great fight -was then waged by the Conservative party-
Remember, this all relates to the fall session of 1919 at which many members of this parliament were present.
A great fight was then waged by the Conservative party to take over these three railway systems that had gone into bankruptcy, reorganize them, consolidate them and make them into a Canadian National railway to be owned by the people of the Dominion of Canada.
Then later on:
Day in and day out in the old museum during the session of 1919 the railway hill was fought to a finish. Every kind and method of opposition was urged against it. Nothing was left undone or unsaid by our opponents.

I remember some of the amendments that were moved on that occasion and I will mention one or two of them. Under the guidance of Mr. Meighen that bill was fought through the house. Amendment after amendment was moved to defeat it. The late Mr. D. D. McKenzie moved that the matter be dropped and not considered for the present time. His motion was defeated. Then came a motion by Mr. Denis, at that time member for Joliette and until recently a member of the house. His motion was defeated. Then there was a motion by the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding to appoint a royal commission to inquire into the whole matter, his object being to defeat the bill and to destroy the government as well. His motion was defeated. After that followed a motion by my right hon. friend the present Prime Minister on the third reading of the bill, just before it was passed, a motion to recommit it to the committee of the whole house, which constituted a want of confidence motion in the government on the third reading. It was intended to defeat the government and to destroy the bill.
Then later:
When the Liberals had exhausted every effort to beat us, when they had tried everything in their power to destroy that measure and prevent the nationalization of these railways, the present Minister of Finance was put up to lead the final attack, and in the early hours of the morning he solemnly moved that the bill be given the six months' hoist. . . The Liberals tried by everything in their power to destroy that measure but they failed. .	. No, Mr. Speaker, hon gentlemen opposite had no faith in a national railway system then, and they tried to kill it at its birth, and for two or three years afterwards they continued their efforts to destroy it.
Now what are the facts? In the first place, my hon. friend says that they were busy with the war; they were straining every nerve to get enough money to carry on the war. He says this of the latter part of the year 1919.
I do not think I need to remind the house that the war ended on, November 11, 1918. The war was over. In the second place, my hon. friend talked all the way through of what the Conservative party were doing at that time. If I am not mistaken the hon. gentleman at that time was boasting that he himself was a Liberal in a Unionist administration. There was no Conservative party in office at the time; the government led by the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden at the time was a unionist government, and in that government, at the time of which my hon. friend speaks, were such gentlemen as himself, Hon. James A. Calder, Hon. Frank Carvell, the Hon. Newton Wesley Rowell, the Hon. A. K. Maclean, all of whom professed at least to be Liberals and meet of whom, I am happy to say, have remained Liberals since. It was not a Conservative government that was in office at that time; it was a unionist administration. Now what about the bill itself to which my hon. friend

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
refers? I say to my hon. friend, and I challenge him to contradict me, that the measure to which he refers was not a Canadian National measure at all, not a measure to organize the Canadian National Railways. The measure with respect to which all these different amendments were made was a " bill for the acquisition of the Grand Trunk Railway Company," a bill a copy of which I have in my hand at the moment. That was the bill which was introduced in that session. And to show bow proud my hon. friends opposite were of the bill they were then introducing, no mention whatever was made of it in the speech from the throne. The session which was being held at that time, as I reminded my hon. friend w'hen he was speaking, was a session called for the purpose of approving the treaty of peace which had been signed at Versailles. That was what the session was for; it was not for the purpose of dealing with a railway measure. And after discussion had taken place on the treaty, this bill for the acquisition of the Grand Trunk Railway was introduced. All the amendments to which my hon. friend has referred, and the object of which he says was to destroy the Canadian National system as we know it to-day, were amendments not one of which was related to any bill respecting the Canadian National system but to the bill respecting the acquisition of the Grand Trunk railway and were introduced by members of the Liberal party because of the terms of the measure as presented to the house and methods taken by hon. gentlemen opposite to achieve their ends. As a matter of fact, as the present Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) reminds me, there was no Canadian National Railway system at that time.
This was the keystone of the arch.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The keystone
of the arch? I am afraid my hon. friend will find that he is the keystone of a very much mistaken statement. My hon. friend makes light of it ait the moment, but all his followers behind him, one after another, repeated the statement over and over again, and I presume we should have heard it repeated from now until after the next general election unless something in the interval had been said respecting the matter.
What was the exact position? Mr. D. D. McKenzie, who was leading the opposition at the time, moved that the bill for the acquisition of the Grand Trunk railway should not be proceeded with at that session inasmuch as the session had been called for the purpose of dealing with the treaty of peace and nothing else. That was the reason of his motion;
it was not as my hon. friend has said, to destroy any railway system. And the motion moved by Mr. Fielding was a motion asking that the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act should be applied to the finances of this particular transaction. That was voted down. My hon. friend says that I sought to destroy the railway system by a motion I introduced. But what was that motion? It was that the agreement between the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the government, which hon. gentlemen opposite were proposing to make by order in council after the close of that session, and which involved more in the way of financial obligation upon this country than any other single transaction in its history, should be referred to parliament for approval before it was acquiesced in. That was the motion, and that was the motion hon. gentlemen opposite voted down. They would not allow the agreement between the company and the government to be submitted to parliament; it was to be put through by order in council, and this notwithstanding that the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway in Great Britain were to have the right to approve it. Hon. gentlemen opposite were obliged later to come to parliament to have it approved, because in drafting the measure they had made some mistake and could not rectify it without bringing the whole measure to the house. To return to the bill and the session of 1919 after my motion was defeated, the present Minister of Finance at the end of that session, moved the six months' hoist, not at all in relation to the Canadian National measure but, as I have said, in regard to this particular transaction introduced at that particular time and in the arbitrary manner I have described.
When was the Canadian National measure introduced? At the previous session of that parliament a measure was brought in to enable the then Canadian Northern railway to be operated along with the Intercolonial railway under one management. That was by a bill entitled " to incorporate the Canadian National Railway Company and respecting the Canadian National Railways." It was assented to in June, 1919, and the bill respecting the Canadian National Railways as passed at that period was, as I have said, nothing more than a bill to enable the Canadian Northern Railway system to be operated along with the Intercolonial. Now my hon. friends the year before had acquired the Canadian Northern system. But how did they acquire it ? They had a royal commission appointed to inquire into the conditions of the railways in this country. That commission made its report, and among other things it stated that the stock of the Cana-

dian Northern system was not worth a single dollar. That was the report of a commission appointed by hon. gentlemen opposite. Yet, on the eve of the election of 1917, these same gentlemen gave to that stock a value of $10,000,000, and forced that transaction through the House of Commons under closure. They got the Canadian Northern into their hands and out of the hands of their friends in that way, and it was to enable them to operate the Canadian Northern along with the government railway that this act respecting the Canadian National Railways was then introduced.
But in speaking of the organization of the Canadian National system such as we have it to-day, may I direct the attention of the house to this further fact. In the bill with respect to the acquisition of the Grand Trunk railway there was not there one clause which related to bringing the Grand Trunk railway system under a Canadian National railway system such as exists to-day? Not a line. As a matter of fact the bill, of which I have a copy, provided that the management of the Grand Trunk Railway Company would remain in England, as had been the case in the past, with the president and the board of directors in that country, and it was not until 1921, when a crisis arose with respect to the arbitration of the Grand Trunk securities, that an agreement was arrived at whereby provision was made for a board of directors in Canada. This board remained a seperate board; it remained the Grand Trunk Railway board and was not brought in any way into association with the Canadian National system. That is what my hon. friend calls the keystone of the whole system, a keystone left absolutely by itself.

So it was, awaiting the
judgment of the privy council.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
To go a step further, what was the position with respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific company, which in March 1919 had been placed in the hands of the Minister of Railways and Canals as a receiver? When the Canadian National bill was passed, when the Grand Trunk bill was passed, no provision was made for ending that receivership and making the Grand Trunk Pacific a part of the system; it was left with the Minister of Railways.
But most significant of all, when the Canadian National bill was before the house and something was said about government ownership, the then Prime Minister, Right Hon. Arthur Meighen was asked whether with respect to railways, the policy of the government was one of government ownership. My
(Mr. Mackenzie King.]
hon. friend, for reasons best known to himself, i n the course of his remarks sought to bring torward Mr. Meighen as the personage above ill others responsible for the present splendid organization of the Canadian National system, yet at the time the bill respecting the National Railways was introduced and Mir. Meighen was asked wihat he had to say about government ownership he absolutely refused to make any commitment. My hon. friend said he came forward with some carefully thought out scheme "a definite plan" he called it, as a matter of fact the whole policy was one of expediency, and there was no vision about it whatever. On April 11, 1919, during the course of the debate, Mr. McMaster put this pointed question to Mr. Meighen, who was then fathering the particular measure under discussion:
I hope the minister will not think me unduly insistent when I ask for a declaration of the policy of the government. Public ownership, whether we wish it or not, has been imposed upon the people. If we were holding the railways only with the idea of disposing of them to private companies in, perhaps, as short a time as possible, one particular kind of organization might be better than another; but if we made up our minds to adopt the permanent policy of the public ownership of railways, some different system of organization would be necessary. The government therefore should state clearly whether they are for the principle of government ownership as a definite policy for Canada.
Then, after mentioning the fact that the responsibility for the principle rested with the government, Mr. McMaster continued:
.... the port that they are steering for should be made known to the people before we are asked to vote for a resolution of this kind.
To this Mr. Meighen replied:
I do not know just how many years ahead the hon. member thinks we should place ourselves in order to determine the port. I think the government is well advised to take its hearings by ports that are in sight, not to fix a policy with reference to yet unborn decades. So far as there is any necessity of stating policy, the government's policy as to railways has been stated and repeated over and over again. As to the roads that we now own, our policy is to continue to own them and to operate them; we have no intention of selling them to any private corporation. Certain roads we do not own.
The Grand Trunk Pacific is one; our policy as to that has been brought down to the house, and we are engaged in the carrying out of that policy. The Grand Trunk is another; we have stated repeatedly our policy as to the Grand Trunk: we have stated what we are doing. The Canadian Pacific is another; the government has not intimated to parliament any intention of acquiring the Canadian Pacific Railway company. I do not know what more the hon. gentleman desires; I certainly do not know what more is necessary to the consideration of

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
this resolution. Every time the subject of railways is mentioned in parliament, is the government, as to its policy, to see years or centuries ahead? All the government has to do is to adjust its course with reference to circumstances now known; we have stated our course with reference to all the railway circumstances now known. All that is necessary to a consideration of this bill is a determination of the question whether it is the part of wisdom to operate such roads as we now and may in the future own under the system set out and by the principle clearly defined in this bill, namely, by the establishment of a holding and operating company, the Canadian Rational Railways.
That is the extent to which Mr. Meighen, who was supposed to have had the far-sighted vision to bring into being the Canadian National system as we have it to-day, was at that time .prepared to commit himself and his party.
May I say that if the government of that day had had the slightest intention of bringing about the organization of the Canadian National Railways as we now know it, that measure would most certainly have received mention in some speech from the throne, but neither in the special session during which the Grand Trunk was acquired nor during the previous session when provision was made for the Canadian Northern being administered along with the Intercolonial as part of a national system was there a single word in the speech from the throne in regard to such a measure. In each case the railway bills were introduced, one might almost say, more or less surreptitiously after the session had commenced. Indeed, the impression was general at the time that the government's object was to return the roads to private control at a convenient season, and under conditions more or less favourable to some of the government's own friends.
What was the position at the end of 1921? As I have said, if hon. gentlemen opposite were so sure of the future of the railways; if they were so proud of their alleged paternity of the railway system, why did they not make a little out of it during the elections in 1921? They did just the opposite; they disowned the whole business, they blamed previous Liberal governments for all the misfortunes of the roads, and the situation as the present government, found it when it came into office was this: Instead of there being any Canadian National Railway system such as we have to-day there were three different railway organizations carrying on, separate and distinct, at that time; the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway was in the hands of the Minister of Railways and Canals as a receiver, and its affairs were being administered through the Department of Railways

and Canals; the Canadian Northern Railway system, together with the Intercolonial Railway, was under the management of a Canadian Northern directorate, not a Canadian National management or directorate, but with a Canadian Northern board of directors appointed under orders in council in 1918. That railway was travelling under an alias; it was called Canadian National but it could not be known legitimately as the Canadian National system because up to that time it had not become a part of such. There was simply a Canadian Northern administration, and in addition there was the separate administration of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, which had its own president and board of directors.
That was necessary until the decision of the privy council was made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The decision of the privy council had been made. My hon. friend will find that it was made before the election. There may have been some appeal on a point of law, but apart from all that, the decision of the privy council had nothing to do with it. My hon. friends had it within their power, had they wished to do so, to pass such legislation as they deemed necessary to bring the Grand Trunk when it was acquired under Canadian National control and which would have relieved them from waiting for any decision of the privy council.
No, we had to wait.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend is quite wrong; he is mistaken.

I am sure the Prime Minister will agree with me that as appeal was taken from the arbitration, parliament could not act pending a decision. I happen to remember that the decision was made after the election, because I was in London when the decision was announced.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Did the decision of the privy council have anything to do with the forming of a Canadian National railway board to run the Canadian Northern?
Absolutely, because if the decision went in accordance with the contentions of the Grand Trunk the matter had to be re-arbitrated.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But that had nothing to do with the Canadian Northern.
Certainly it had, because the two systems could not be combined until after the decision was rendered.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Surely my hon. friend is not familiar with what took place.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Then if he is familiar with it he does not like the whole business. I venture to say that even to-day my hon. friend would not support the action of the government of the day in giving $10,000,000 to Mackenzie and Mann for the common stock of the Canadian Northern System. It was that $10,000,000 that brought the Canadian Northern under the control of the government, and it was to administer that particular road that the act to which I have referred was passed in the early part of 1919 or other roads which might be amalgamated. That act when it was passed had nothing to do with the Grand Trunk at all; it simplv united the Canadian Northern with the government road for the purposes of administrit tion.

I merely point out again that there could be no union between these two systems until after the decision of the privy council had been announced. With respect to the payment of $10,000,000, I declined to follow Mr. Pugsley and the Liberal party in giving them $40,000,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend speaks about there having been no unity between the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Northern until a decision was given by the privy council. Whether that is or is not true does not affect in the least the fact that the Canadian National Act was passed in relation to the Canadian Northern railway and the Intercolonial railway, to bring the two under the one management. Even that much had not been done when the present government came into office in December, 1921, although the bill had passed during the early part of 1919. We found on coming into office two separate systems, and we also found the Grand Trunk Pacific being administered by a receiver. We realized that the first thing to be done was to end this duplication, this dual, if not triple control, to bring about a centralized control and to discover the right person to put in charge of the two systems when they were combined. In November, 1922, we succeeded in obtaining the services of Sir Henry Thornton, whose reputation at that time as a manager of railways in the old country was outstanding. If any one person above everyone else, is entitled to credit for the present success of the Canadian National system, I venture to say that that person is Sir Henry Thornton. But I think Sir Henry Thornton would be the first to admit that along with him should be associated the Minister of Railways and Canals who was in office at the time he came to

this country, and the ministers who have been in office and have been associated with him in the work of administration. Too much credit cannot be given to the late Hon. William C. Kennedy, the first Minister of Railways and Canals in this administration; to the Right Hon. George P. Graham, and to Hon. Charles A. Dunning, the present Minister of Railways and Canals for the manner in which they have cooperated with Sir Henry Thornton and his board of directors and dealt with the affairs of the National railways in this parliament. Great credit should also be given to the officials of the railway for the loyal manner in which they have cooperated with Sir Henry, and credit as well to every man employed upon the system. They are the persons to whom credit is due for the success of the Canadian National railways, and not the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen or the hon. gentlemen opposite. So far as any government is entitled to credit it is the present administration which brought about the complete unification of the lines, secured and appointed the president and board of directors, and -which along with Sir Henry Thornton, has walked out the -best, type of organization -best suited, and has kept the system from political interference.
My hon. friend spoke about extravagance, and he brought up a number of items which he claimed were in the nature of extravagances on the part of the administration. He mentioned the legations at Washington, Paris and Tokyo. With regard to the legation at Washington, he said that the government had spent $500,000 on a palace for the present minister, to be used as a place of residence, whereas the government should have allowed him to rent or buy a house for himself. My *hon. friend knows that such is not a true statement. He knows that the building which has been purchased at Washington was not purchased as a residence, but for the purpose of a legation, including the offices of the legation as well as a residence for the minister. He knows that practically all the ministers or ambassadors at Washington live in buildings which are either embassies or legations. My 'hon. friend instead of being penurious in his criticism might have been generous enough to have said that the present minister the Hon. Vincent Massey, deserves the highest praise not only of all political parties in this house but of the nation as a whole for the manner in which he has represented the interests of this Canada, at Washington. He should receive the highest praise not only for the manner in which he has represented the interests of this country, but for the very generous manner in which he has placed a considerable portion of his own private for-

tune at the service of tihe state. Anyone who knows anything about the manner in which Mr. Massey has been carrying on the representation of Canada tit Washington knows that whatever he has received from the government is only a small portion of what he has spent. His private means 'have been given liberally towards helping to maintain the reputation of Canada at Washington on the high plane which it holds in the estimation of the people of this continent. Instead of misrepresenting the situation with respect to the legation building, my hon. friend might well have directed his talents to a be'tter end.
He took the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) up to the White House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And I have no doubt he would take my hon. friend there also.
No, he will not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think they would let my hon. friend in.
He will never do that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Not only is
this building being used for office purposes, but in the purchase made the furnishings for residential purposes were acquired as well. The amount which my hon. friend mentioned was in excess of the cost of the building and site, including the cost of furnishings. The hon. member for South Wellington also said:
Last year the vote to maintain our Washington embassy was $60,000; to-day it stands in the estimates at $100,000-an unwarrantable and extravagant increase of $40,000.
My hon. friend knows that that is not correct. The vote last year was not $60,000; the vote was for $100,000, and the vote the year before was for $130,000. I told the house in the session of 1927-28 that if it would sanction the purchase of a legation building at Washington we would cut that estimate from $130,000 to $100,000, and we have kept that promise. The estimates included an amount of $100,000 last year, and the amount being asked for this year is $100,000, and yet my hon. friend tells the house and the country that there has been unwarranted extravagance in an increase of the vote from $60,000 to $100,000.
In reference to Paris, my hon. friend mentioned an expenditure of $75,000, and then remarked on an additional sum of $40,000 which he said was being provided for another building. He should be careful before he makes such statements. He should look up the records and see what the expenditures are related to. The expenditure of $40,000 was not for another building in addition to and
in connection with the present legation. My hon. friend knows that while Commissioner General, the present minister occupied premises in one part of Paris, which premises were entirely different from those of the legation which we now have in that city. The expenditure of $40,000 to which he referred and led the house to believe was an added extravagance was an amount expended upon premises occupied by the minister while he was the Commissioner General, and during which time no money was being spent upon a legation 'building. There was in his Statement a complete 'misrepresentation of the facts. We come next to the building at London. My hon. friend considers the expenditure upon that building as an extravagance, but I wonder if the people of Canada are not proud of the Canadian building in London. Every dominion of the British Empire has a building in London: New Zealand has one, Australia has one and South Africa has one, and I know that some of the buildings which are occupied by other dominions in London are much more expensive than the offices which we have. We have been fortunate in securing for our offices the finest site in London; we have been fortunte in obtaining a very good building there, and I think this country has reason to be proud of the purchase which the government has made. My hon. friend referred to the cost of administration of the High Commissioner's office, and compared it to the cost during the time his government was in office; he said:
When I was in the Meighen government the vote for the whole establishment in London was $69,000; this year the vote is $117,000.
He is again guilty of a very serious oversight, if not of a deliberate misrepresentation, because when he gave the figure as to what the London office cost when he was in the government he deliberately omitted the salaries paid, although, when giving the figures with reference to the present government, he included them. My hon. friend apparently took the figures as shown in the statement of 1920-21, which are as follows: Supply, government contingencies, $69,586. That is the $69,000 which he said was the cost of the whole establishment in London when he was in the government. But right alongside that figure in the public accounts of that year stand the following;
High Commissioner's publications.... $ 1,000 Supplementary, civil government contingencies	 7,000
Civil government salaries	 25,950
These figures give a total of $103,536, and not the $69,000 as given by my hon. friend. At that time the High Commissioner's office

These are all additional branches of activities that have been gathered into the present office in London.
Now we come to Ottawa, and my hon. friend says: " Here again there has been an absolute waste. The destruction of property, destroyed for what? Merely to get a view." My hon. friend knows better than that. He knows first of all that the property in Ottawa that was demolished was for the most part in the nature of old buildings that were to have been taken down anyway. That is the reason why at i'he particular time the government took the step it did. We knew that these buildings were to be demolished. The old Russell House block had been for the most part disposed of; it was to 'be torn down, and it was a question of either acquiring the property for the state at that time or losing the opportunity of getting it later on because of the more expensive buildings that would certainly have been put up there. My hon. friend knows further that this House of Commons in general, if not in specific terms, approved of something being done to commemorate in the capital of the Dominion the diamond jubilee of confederation, and this particular commemoration was to take the form of a confederation park in the centre of the city, provided the civic authorities were prepared to cooperate with the government in the matter. He knows that an arrangement has been reached between the government and the city authorities for a very considerable improvement in the heart of the capital, a much needed improvement in the immediate vicinity of these houses of parliament which means much in the present but which will mean infinitely more in the future. He knows very well that what has been done in that regard has been done as part of a great scheme in the national interest and not, as he says, for the purpose of getting a view. I think hon. gentlemen opposite would be more public-spirited, more patriotic, to say the least, if instead of criticizing the government on every conceivable subject, they would recognize that there are some questions that might well be taken out of the realm of party discussion altogether. Improvement of the capital of this Dominion is one of those questions, and I say now to my hon. friend opposite I think the step he should take-and I am prepared to have him take iit and to cooperate if he is agreeable so to do-would be to have a group of hon. fMr. Mackenzie King.]
gentlemen behind him or who are associated with him, meet with myself and a corresponding group of hon. members on this side together with representatives of the other group apposite, and discuss plans for the further improvement of the capital of this country. Let us then come to this parliament and say what we feel is owing alike to the present and the future generations and needed in order to make the capital of our country what we would like to have it and what we know future generations would wish it to be.
The talk about extravagance in the price of public buildings mentioned, reminds me of the discussion we had in this parliament with respect to the completion of the tower of these Houses of Parliament. Hon. gentlemen who were here then will remember that for two days the government, on an item which asked the house for enough money to complete the present tower, was held up on the score that the tower might well remain as it was and that we had better wait until the country was in a more favourable position. Notwithstanding the fact that the whole front of the parliament buildings was obscured by the equipment required in the reconstruction of the building, we were told that the completion of the tower might well wait; that we were too extravagant. This present opposition is pretty much on a par with that; only it is not a tower, it is the capital of the Dominion that is involved. We owe it to the country as a whole to make this capital worthly of this great Dominion and I may tell my hon. friends opposite that they will find in the hearts of the people in the back concessions much more pride in the capital of their country than they themselves have exhibited in the discussions in this house.
I might give the house a little information with respect to some of our expenditures. Consider the building at the comer of Sussex and Rideau streets, the so called1 Daly building, a hideous looking structure, an eyesore in the city, It was purchased by hon. gentlemen opposite, not for $500,000, as my hon. friend says the legation building at Washington, a very handsome building with furnishings complete was purchased for, .but purchased for $1,000,000, and on what further terms? That $100,000 should be paid down on the eve of the election of 1921, and that from then on the sum of $100,000 should be paid each year with interest on the balance at the rate of 6 per cent per annum. Under that contract we have been obliged to pay $100,000 and to contribute 6 per cent on the balance each year from, the time hon. gentlemen opposite went out of office until to-day, and the payments will not be completed until next year.

The payment when completed will amount, to $1270,000. These are the bon. gentlemen who talk about waste and extravagance.
May I refer again ,to what I have just said about the purchase of the Canadian Northern system? Hon. gentlemen apposite had a report from their own commission which said that the common stock of the Canadian Northern was not worth a single cent, but notwithstanding that they so engineered matters as to give to that stock a value of $10,000,000 and compelled the people of this oowntry to meet that amount out of taxes 'by the use of closure in this House of Commons.
That was done by arbitration.

speechtext: What could we not do with $10,000,000 in the improvement of the .capital of Canada? That money would be better in the treasury here for the improvement of Ottawa than in the pockets of friends of my hon. friends opposite.
The right hon. gentleman knows that was awarded by arbitration by Chief Justice Meredith.

speechtext: My hon. friend can make his statement later.

I was not there. It was

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I daresay my hon. friend thanks the Lord he was not there May I now conclude what I have to say?
I had intended to say something about tirade and the tariff, in regard to which my hon. friend spoke at same length, but I shall have to leave that for some later time. I should like however to say a few words in regard to the amendments to the motion that has been made by the Minister of Finance that the house go into committee of ways and means.
During the last few years on each occasion that the Minister of Finance has brought in his budget, we have been confronted, as regularly as by the years themselves, with amendments of hon. gentlemen opposite, amendments which were diametrically opposite in character. We have had one amendment which has asked us to increase taxation, to raise the tariff, to give more in the way of protection; and we have had from the other end of the chamber an amendment for less in the way of taxation, for reduction in customs duties, for less in the way of protection. On each occasion we have met those amendments by pointing out that it was the policy of the government to pursue a moderate course, avoiding an extreme in one direction as well as an extreme in the other, to take only that course which would help to bring prosperity to this country. Our course is vindicated by the position of the country at the present time. We have the prosperity at which we have aimed, and we intend to maintain it and, if possible, to increase it. We intend to maintain and increase it by exactly the same methods as those we have adopted in the past. To-day we are confronted with amendments similar to those of previous years. If we take the amendment of hon. gentlemen opposite and strip it of its verbiage, what does it mean? More in the way of taxation, higher tariffs, more in the way of protection. On the other hand, hon. gentlemen at the other end of the chamber ask us to go a little further in reducing taxation, in reducing duties and to do much less in the way of protection.
This year differs from other years in one essential particular. This year, when the government was preparing its budget, it had before it the knowledge which is common throughout the continent, that a neighbouring country was about to make certain changes in its tariff, changes which may materially affect trade between the two countries. Trade between this country and the United States is,
I believe, the greatest trade that exists between any two countries in the world, and naturally we are interested in what the citizens of the republic do with respect to matters which may affect that trade. We are interested as well in all that affects the industrial conditions of that country because, as we know from experience, matters are so interrelated in economic affairs that it is seldom that one portion of this continent is appreciably affected by depression or the opposite without other parts being also affected. We have the word of those in authority in the neighbouring republic that there are certain measures to be introduced at a special session of congress now about to assemble. An important measure, we are led to believe, is a measure relating to farm relief. Another measure relates to "limited adjustments of the tariff"; that I think is the expression which has been officially used. Having that knowledge 'before us, I ask hon. gentlemen irrespective of party: In the condition of prosperity which Canada is to-day enjoying would it be desirable on the part of the administration to take any action with respect to the tariff in Canada at the present time which by those across the line who may be interested in seeking to raise the tariff in that country could be regarded as provocative? I say that with the knowledge which we have before
