The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
us at the present time, were we to do what hon. gentlemen opposite by their amendment apparently wish us to do, namely raise the tariff, we would be creating in the minds of the American people the very sentiment which would cause them to raise their tariff higher perhaps than it was ever their intention to raise it. We do not intend to take any action of that provocative character.
May I say to my hon. friends opposite, in the other comer of the house, that were we to-day to take a step along the lines of increasing the British preference to a greater degree than exists at the present time that step also might be misconstrued, for we know that there are people on the other side of the line who are just as anxious to be troublemakers as certain people on this side of the line, who are ready to misrepresent matters, and we have to take human nature as it is, and deal with it as it is. So facing the situation before us, we have followed the policy that we have followed in the past and that we shall follow at all times, of dealing with each situation as it arises in the light of the conditions as they exist at the time.
That is the position which this government took when we came into charge of the administration of the country's affairs. What did we find? We found the depressed condition that Canada was then in. We had before us the record of hon. gentlemen opposite, where year after year deficits were exhibited in the public accounts. We took the step that was necessary to deal with that situation. We put on some extra taxation so that we might be able to balance the budget and restore public confidence in the public finances of the country. The moment we had restored public confidence and balanced the budget we began to remove taxation, and to remove it steadily. We saw that if the country was to prosper, what was needed above all else was that the basic industries of the country should be made prosperous, that production should be increased. So we dealt next with the duties on the implements of production in the great basic industries. Later on there were other changes that we felt should be made, and all along, year after yeair, whilst moving steadily in the direction of lower tariffs and taxation, we have consistently followed a policy of dealing with each situation as it existed at the time in the light of all known circumstances, hoping always that by so doing we might further the prosperity which we enjoy at the present time. I say that that is exactly what wre intend to do with respect to any situation that may arise in the future.

Hon. gentlemen opposite have been very crafty in some of itheir methods in debate. This year they have been perhaps a little more subtle than before. They have not wished to refer to the past, and above all else they have sought to avoid the present, and so they have sought to create-and thi3 is what we have had all through this debate- a discussion not with respect to an existing situation but with respect to something that may oir may not happen next year. They have resorted to the device of shifting discussion from the present issue and fighting in advance an imaginary tariff war. They have told us that this and that should be done, not because something is 'being done at the moment, but because something may be done by the government of the United States next year or during the present year. They have conjured up and talked of tariff wars. They have suggested that special sessions of parliament should be called. They have urged that legislation on the tariff should be by orders in council; they have talked about a red-blooded attitude on the part of Canada, They have chosen their ground well, because if there is one thing above another that hon. gentlemen 'opposite are adepts at, it is jingoist pronouncements, more particularly when they relate to the United States. But may I say to my hon. friends opposite, it is not a red-hlooded attitude that is needed at the present moment so much as a coolheaded attitude, and a cool-headed attitude is the attitude which this administration has taken with regard to all tariff matters from the time it came into office, and is the attitude which we intend to continue to take during the time we are serving the people in the position which we now occupy.
May I quote to the house the two amendments that are before us. First of all, may I make this clear, that each of them, though they differ so widely, as I have indicated, are alike at least in this particular, that each is in the nature of a want of confidence motion in the administration. The Minister of Finance has asked that the house should have leave to consider ways and means of raising the revenue necessary to carry on the government of the country. Hon. gentlemen immediately opposite say: No, we will not allow this motion to carry; we ask instead that there shall be increased protection. Hon. gentlemen at the other end of the house say: No, we will not permit the house to consider ways and means; we want the government to go back and consider the question of increasing tihe British preference. My hon. friends know, or they ought to know, that if their motions were to carry, the government would not be

aible to consider the very questions they put before us, for the simple reason that the government would no longer be in power, having been denied the right of providing the ways and means of carrying on the administration of the country's affairs. I think that should be understood by the country in viewing the action of my hon. friends when they come to vote on their amendments.
Why allow any amendment at all to this budget?

It is interesting to notice what has happened with respect to hon. gentlemen, opposite on the question of the tariff. During the election of 1921 and the election of 1925 and the election of 1926, we heard from hon. gentlemen opposite endless talk about the necessity for increased protection. That was openly and avowedly the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite-increased protection. Wherever they went they talked about the need of increased protection. If they went into a mining district, it was the mining industry that needed protection. If they went into a manufacturing centre, it was the manufacturing industries that needed protection. If they went into a farming district, it was some branch of agriculture or horticulture that needed protection. Wherever they went they always preached protection in relation to the industries of the particular locality. But they did not succeed in 1921; they did not succeed in 1925, and they got a knockout blow in 1926, with the result that immediately afterwards they dropped the word "protection" completely. They had their convention at Winnipeg and they drew up their tariff program, but you can search from one end to the other of that platform and you will not find the word protection" in the whole of it; there is no mention of it, they talk of the "historical fiscal policy of the Liberal-Conservative party." The idea was there, to be sure, but it was disguised. The action of bon. gentlemen opposite reminds one of something that Lord Asquith said in the last speech which he made as leader of the Liberal party in England. In reviewing the work which the Liberal party had accomplished in the period of his leadership, he referred to an election that bad taken place in Great Britain in 1905,
I think it was, when the forces of protection were so completely routed that thereafter, protection on the part of its advocates never raised its head, but according to Lord Asquith,
" went creeping about under modest and belittling pseudonyms"
They talked first, of " tariff reform " then of " safeguarding," but studiously avoided the use of the word " protection." That is exactly what hon. gentlemen opposite have been doing here with respect to the word " protection ". Their course has not even the merit of originality; it is a. belated imitation of an old country pseudonym. Look at this resolution. They have got here the word "safeguarding", and they have been careful to place it in front of the word that relates more specifically to protection, to sort of shelter it; and they do not even use the word "protection", 'but the word "protecting", afraid to come out with a substantive but as a means of declaring their intention 'having resort to a participle. Let me read this resolution:
This house regrets that the financial proposals of the government make no provision for reasonably safeguarding and protecting-

But after the session was over my hon. friend found the forces around him had been too strong. So

Now, may I say a word to my hon. friends at the far end of this chamber with respect to their particular amendment. As they well know, the British preference has been a part of the policy of the Liberal party from the days when Sir Wilfrid Laurier introduced in the parliament of this country the first measure of British preference. This Dominion of Canada has led the empire in the matter of the British preference; and the Liberal party has led Canada. Year after year we have considered carefully wherein we could justifiably extend and increase the British preference. And may I say to my hon. friends, we intend to continue so to do from this time onward. I want no misunderstanding as to why we have to reject their resolution. It is not because we are not strongly in favour of the British preference. It is not because we have not considered it. We have made some increase in the British preference in the present budget. But I have to tell my hon. friends quite frankly, and I think they must in their hearts agree with me, that there are strong reasons why in this session above all sessions we should do as little as possible by way of change in the tariff. That we believe is the wisest course to pursue.
Next session we will, as I have already said, deal with the situation as we find it at that 
particular time. And we will deal with it in the interests of Canada. The Minister of Finance has, I think, in a few brief words, made very clear what the position of the government is in this matter. In so far as we have a fiscal problem, our task would appear to be that of readjusting, as necessity arises, our customs tariff schedules to meet new conditions, other things being equal, of favouring those countries which favour our products. It is our desire to trade freely with any and all who are willing to trade with us. What may, or may not, be possible in this particular necessarily depends in some measure on the purchasing power and the fiscal policies of other countries.^ The policy of this administration is not a high tariff policy; it is a low tariff policy. Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks may I congratulate the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) who spoke so eloquently this afternoon, in what was without doubt a very masterful speech which did credit to him as the Prime Minister of this country and as the leader of one of the historic political parties of Canada. I shall not attempt to follow the argument of the right hon. gentleman; his speech was devoted to a comparison of a government, his own, exercising power in times of peace, with a government headed by a Conservative leader exercising power in time of war. I shall not attempt to follow him in his argument for the simple reason that I do not consider the Prime Minister a very good authority on the difficulties, financial and otherwise, which confront a government in this country in time of war. My reason for that statement is that during those fearful days when the people of Canada were concerned only with winning the.war the right hon. gentleman who to-day criticized the war government was devoting

his splendid talents to the work of ironing out difficulties for the Rockefeller Institute in the United States. Consequently I do not consider him a good authority on the difficulties confronting a government in time of war.
Since I am in a congratulatory mood, Mr. Speaker, and since I will not be in that mood long, I am reminded that it is an amenity of parliament to congratulate a minister of finance upon the presentation of his budget. Even at this late date I intend no violence to such an ancient and honourable custom, but when I congratulate my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on the present budget I must perforce explain that it is courtesy and not reason that motivates my action. In Canada we are accustomed to consider the budget from two distinct aspects: on the one hand as a tabulation of fiscal and trade figures, and on the other as an indication of public policy. Judged from the first viewpoint the present budget is in many respects satisfactory; it records a year of abounding revenues, something like $450,000,000 having been collected. But, Mr. Speaker, estimable gentleman though the Minister of Finance may be, he is not a wizard; he does not raise these revenues by waving some magic wand. There is only one source from wdiich they come; there is only one way in which they are derived. That source is the people of Canada and that way is taxation, and when my hon. friends make the welkin ring with references to the fact that they have collected $450,000,000 in the form of revenue from the people of this country I point out to them that 90 per cent of that money was collected from the pockets of the taxpayers, either directly or indirectly, in the form, of taxation. I also point out to them that this is the first occasion since 'Canadian confederation was consummated on which any government, Grit or Tory, has taken such an amount of money in one fiscal year from the people by way of taxation. My hon. friends may take what comfort they can from that declaration. I do not know whether they are entitled to bouquets because of that fact; if there are any bouquets to be handed out I will allow the taxpayers to give them to the Minister of Finance.
One would have thought, Mr. Speaker, that there would be a considerable reduction in taxes in view of the revenues which have been derived; one would have expected that these revenues would have been applied in order to reduce the taxes of the poor, common people of this country. But let us see what has happened. Whatever reductions have been

The Budget-Mr. Macdougall
made have been entirely in favour of the *wealthy people of this country at the expense of the poorer people. There is a canon of taxation that has been recognized by every government in every part of the civilized world; economists term it the canon of human welfare. Briefly it means that the strongest backs shall bear the heaviest burdens, that those who can best afford to pay shall pay the most, and that where relief is to be given, it shall be given those who need it most. The Minister of Finance, in his present budget, has completely violated that ancient, honourable and most equitable canon of taxation, because whatever relief is accorded in this budget by way of reduced taxation goes to those who can best afford to pay taxes.
That has been his policy in previous years; during a former session in his budget he took off the duty on angostura bitters so that the rich men of this country might have their cocktails a little cheaper; now he has reduced the tax on pullman car tickets and on telegrams and cablegrams. All these reductions affect only the rich men who can well afford to pay and should pay these taxes, but of what assistance are they to the man on the farm, the man who works in the mine, the man who goes down to the sea in ships, the artisans and workingmen of Canada? Abso-'utely of no assistance whatever.
The Prime Minister has to-day repeated the claim which has been made by his supporters with regard to the prosperity of Canada. There is no doubt whatever that there is prosperity in Canada; there will be prosperity under any government, because the great natural resources with which we are endowed are of such a nature that even the government in office cannot prevent prosperity from coming to this country, much as they may try and they have been trying ever since they assumed office in 1921. We must not judge the prosperity of a country by the reported surpluses in national bookkeeping; we must not judge the prosperity of a country by the reports issued by the large financial institutions. If you desire to find out whether a country is really prosperous you must not go into the mart, to the financial institutions nor to the mansions of the rich; you must go to the homes of the common people and find out how much the sum total of the human value of happiness and contentment has been increased for them by the policies of the government in power. There is considerable philosophy in those lines of the poet Markham in which he says:
We all are blind until we see That in the common plan,
Nothing is worth the making That does not make the man.
Why build these temples glorious If man unbuilded goes,
We build a world in vain unless The builder also grows.
How have the builders of this country, our farmers, our fishermen, our miners and our labouring classes fared under the policy of this government? There are only two ways by which the policies of this government can assist the common people of Canada: one is by reducing the cost of living, and the other is by putting more money into their pay envelopes. What about the rate of wages since this government assumed office? I make the statement, and I challenge contradiction from any supporter of the government, that in every industry employing over two hundred men wages have been reduced since this government came into power in 1921. Not only have they been reduced, but in some cases the reduction has amounted to as much as fifty per cent. So far as the money which goes into their pay envelopes is concerned, the workmen are worse off under the policies of this government. But someone may reply,
" Thev may have benefited in the matter of real wages; the money wage is not important, it is what you can buy with what you get." Well do I remember the right hon. the Prime Minister-and I do not, think he mentioned it in his speech this afternoon-discussing the cost of living while he was in opposition in 1920. I heard him in one of the theatres in Halifax while he was discussing that issue with a sob in his voice and a tear in his eye. He told of how the people were being crushed by the high cost of living, and how he and his government would reduce it. He has been in power since 1921; he has been carrying on his policy of fiscal folly, and what is the result? The result is that ten years after the cessation of war the cost of living is just a little higher to-day than it was at _ the time he made bis pathetic speech >in Halifax.
Let us now consider the second phase of a budget, namely, the indication of public policy. There has been no indication of a policy of any kind so far as the fiscal condition of Canada is concerned. They do not preach free trade; they do not preach protection-they know not where they stand, but they occupy that invidious position which was so vigorously condemned by our divine Lord when he said, "So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth."
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) mentioned this fiscal question in his speech

The Budget-Mr. Macdougall
of yesterday. At this point I might say, in common with all the members of the house, that I am glad to see him again in his place in the house. He brought out a new argument in favour of free trade, in which, by the way, he does not believe. He said that the imposition of customs duties would only mean war; that the nations which raised their tariff to protect their own people, to protect their own markets for their own products, to protect their own workmen in their jobs, were paving the way for a world war. He went further and said that the policy of high tariff was condemned at the economic conference at Geneva through a resolution which was passed there condemning the policy of tariff protection. Of course it was. Why? Because those who were assembled there knew that it wias a pious resolution and one which would not amount to anything. The delegates knew that the tariff was a question of internal policy, and they knew that when they had subscribed to this pious free trade resolution they could go back, as was the case with the United States delegates, and put into effect a tariff policy which would suit the needs of their own people and protect their own markets. My 'hon. friend seemed to take some pride in the fact that Canada, through its delegates, had been able to announce at that Geneva conference that it was the only country in the world, with the possible exception of soviet Russia, which had reduced its tariff. Then he turned around and said in effect that because we had acted differently from every other country we must be right. He puts me in mind of the fond mother who was watching a battalion of soldiers marching by. She proudly said to one of her neighbours, "See, they are all out of step but my Johnny!" The Minister of Justice seems to think that all the other countries of the world have all been wrong, and that Canada alone has been right. I ask him to contemplate the other side of the question; perhaps the rest of the world is right and Canada is wrong.
I am one of those who believe that a country like Canada, with its great diversity of natural resources, is required to maintain definitely the protective principle in its fiscal policy. In Canada we have a country unsurpassed in natural wealth. We have the wealth of farm, forest, sea and mine. We have the potentialities of becoming a great economic and industrial people. We have the opportunities to develop a wealth sufficient to maintain a population of one hundred million people within the confines of our country. When we consider a fiscal question,
HVIr. Macdougall.]
we must not look through the eyes of days nor yet of years; when we are legislating in respect to a matter of policy of this kind, we must look through the eyes of centuries; we must realize that we have an obligation to those who come after us and thus be ever ready to make even a little sacrifice, if that be necessary, to apply the protective principle for the sake of developing our own industries and making us, as far as possible, independent economically of foreign powers. Even before he 'became leader of the Tory party, when he was still High Commissioner in London, Sir Charles was actively engaged in furthering the policy launched by Joseph Chamberlain as a protective policy for the British Empire. As everybody knows, Chamberlain's dream was to organize the British Empire on the pattern of the German empire

not the liberal-minded German empire, but the Tory, Prussianized fabric which aimed at creating economic as well as military domination on the continent of Europe. Chamberlain, so aptly described by Gladstone as the first English politician of the Yankee type, wanted to induce the English people to imitate at once the Yankee policy and the Prussian policy. One 'of his main arguments was that the British Empire should be self-sustaining in matters economic just as was the German empire and the great American commonwealth. Sir Charles Tupper caught that idea with enthusiasm, and became an apostle of inter-imperial preferential trade as advocated by Chamberlain.
This was the position when the general election of 1896 took place. Three years before, the Liberal party, at their famous national convention hel.d here in Ottawa, had pledged themselves to the wiping out of every vestige of protection. But when the general election came they accepted subscriptions from the manufacturers' association. Therefore once the election was over they had to make a composition between their preelection pledges against protection and the pro-election assistance they had received from the people interested in maintaining protection. It was then that they caught up that cunning device of the British preference, which on the one hand they offered to the " free trade on principle " Liberals as a reduction of the tariff, and on the other hand to the protected manufacturers as an obstacle to any further reduction in the tariff. The difference between the preferential policy as advocated by Joseph Chamberlain and Sir Charles Tupper, and the British preference as adopted by the Liberal government of Canada in 1897 was this: The genuine article was to be a protective policy for the whole British Empire; as adopted by the Liberal government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier it was a protective policy for British capital, for British industry and for British labour, as against Canadian capital, Canadian labour and Canadian industry. As a matter of fact it worked out largely in that

way, with the result that all or most of the complaints that arose from the industrial sections, at least in the province of Quebec, as against foreign competition, arose from the operation of the preferential tariff.
Was protection in Sir Wilfrid Laurier's mind when he introduced the British preference in 1897?

I cannot say. I never
try to find out what is in people's minds. I simply try to put a reasonable construction upon their actions. The policy advocated by -the fullfl-edged imperialis(t Tory protectionist was an all-round tariff for the whole British Empire. The policy as devised and applied by the Liberal government of 1897 was a combination of their pre-election free trade principles and of the Tory imperialist protective policy. It worked to this effect, that it not only enabled the British manufacturer to take advantage of it as against foreign competition in Canada, but also enabled some skilful English agents of continental manufacturers to have goods made in France, -but more especially in Belgium, Holland and Germany, finished to about 85 or 90 per cent, brought into England, marked as British goods, and entered as such into Canada under the preferential tariff. That practice was inaugurated about 1899-1900, and it has continued ever since. So that this so-called policy tending towards freer trade resulted as a matter of fact in a measure of protection for the British manufacturer, for the British trades agent, for the Dutch manufacturer, for the Belgian manufacturer and for the French manufacturer. There is only one class of industrialists that has not benefited by it, and that is the Canadian industrialists. From the moment this was discovered there was a tendency on the part of the Liberal government of that day to revise their policy. As a matter of fact, at the imperial conference of 1902, Mr. Fielding served notice upon the British government that unless, by some measure of reciprocity, they implemented their recognition of the advances made by the Canadian parliament and the Canadian people, the Canadian government would revise their policy in favour of the Canadian producer. This was never done except in minor instances.

We need not frame our policy to suit or to antagonize the Americans or to suit or antagonize the British or any other people on earth. It was a foolish thing to introduce the factor of sentiment into our fiscal policy in 1897; it would be just as foolish to introduce another form of sentiment, wicked sentiment this time, against the United States, in any change we may make in that policy. Let us play our game according to our own situation and our own strength. If the American market is to be closed to us to a greater extent than is the case to-day, I suggest, not as a set policy but as one of the factors of our economic situation which always must be in the minds of the men who are responsible for our government, that they must prepare to find some other markets. It was first offered to Great Britain because of the trade relations with her, and there was no objection to that, although Great Britain did not give us anything in return in those days. The British treated us just as they treated the Americans or any other people, because they had the sense to frame their fiscal policies according to the needs of their economic life and not according to some foolish outburst of sentiment. This is one of the many things we have to learn from the people on the other side.

He advocated some kind of reform of the senate, as he has done in this house, and he had an example before him-I think he must have been a teacher at one time, because he believes in teaching by example. He had on the platform with him a senator who has since gone to his reward, and after the Prime Minister had said, "I have appointed this man with strings to him, and I can pull them at any time. Ho must support any legislation that I may propose for the reform of the senate," this senator got up and said, " Yes, that is correct. I was appointed under those conditions." A fine way for the members of the other chamber, who are supposed to sit as judges in the land, to be appointed, that when " Bunty pulls the strings " they will obey his order. Right in this house in 1924 the Prime Minister made a characteristic grandstand gesture in regard to reforming the senate. He told the country prior to the opening of the session that the government were considering legislation looking to a curtailment of the powers of the senate, but that the government were anxious that the country should be convinced of the necessity before pressing it on the attention of parliament. He assured the House of Commons:
I desire to assure the house that when parliament reassembles steps will be taken by the government to obtain, if 'possible, means whereby bills may be enacted by and with the advice and consent of the House of Commons un-v- ^Editions similar in principle to those which have been sanctioned by the parliament of the United Kingdom.
He was asked by the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen just what steps he proposed to take, and the Prime Minister declared that the government would consider the matter during the recess." Well, the recess 'passed, the house opened, and the Prime Minister informed the house that he proposed to call a conference with the provinces upon the question. Near the end of the session, on June 18, 1925, Mr. Meighen again asked whether the government had anything to lay before the proposed conference, and the Prime Minister replied that the government had considered no recommendations and had nothing to offer, but would take up the matter in the recess. Mr. Speaker, I believe it is usually in order to congratulate the preceding speaker, and I desire to take this opportunity to pay tribute to my good friend from North Huron (Mr. Spotton). I am always interested in his speeches and particularly in the dramatic manner of his delivery. If one did not know the other side he probably would take a literal interpretation of his whole speech.
My hon. friend made an accusation against the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott), claiming that the minister was unfair to the constituency represented by my hon. friend. On behalf of the Minister of Public Works I want to say he is not that type of man; I think our Conservative friends are in a position to know that full well, because within one year they tried on three occasions to defeat him in his own riding. At each election he increased his majority; the last election gave him a majority of 2,660, and I think any candidate who opposes him at the next election will proibaibly lose his deposit. I want to say that we new and inexperienced members from southern Ontario owe a great deal to the Minister of Public Works; any one of us would rise to his defence on an occasion of this kind.
The hon. member for North Huron went further and made some caustic references to the Prime Minister of this country. This afternoon we heard the Prime Minister deliver an address which in my opinion was a masterpiece; I do not think any man could add to or take away from that speech. Today, despite all the unfair criticism of the Tory press in years past, the Prime Minister stands high in the estimation of the people of Canada, and after he appeals to the country at the next general election I think our Conservative friends will be found still gazing with longing eyes at the treasury benches across the floor of the house. I think the Prime Minister has demonstrated in no uncertain way that he is well able to emulate our grand old chief, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, especially in the way he picks his cabinet, because we feel that the men who grace the treasury benches at present are the ablest and best body ever to hold office in the history of this country.
I say this government need have no fear with regard to what may happen at another general election, because they are carrying out a policy applicable to the needs of this growing young country. During the last three general elections our Conservative friends appealed on the old protectionist platform, but on each occasion they came back in the minority. The policy applicable to the needs of Canada certainly is one of trade expansion, and I want to say that that policy is being well carried out by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm). That fact is demonstrated by his successful negotiation of trade treaties with many countries throughout the world, so that now our goods are moving freely into the world markets. We do not need to go back very far in history to ascertain how the restricted trade policy brought grief to this country; each time our Conservative friends were in office they created such hard times that we had economic revolts, especially in the rural sections, as witness the formation of the Grange Patrons of Industry and the United Farmers of Ontario. In order to ascertain the effects of such a policy we need only point to the sad plight of the American farmers, due to the fact that they subscribed to the very doctrine expounded by our Conservative friends here. Because of the trade policy of this government I think we are probably the most prosperous country in the world.
But of course our Conservative friends shout hard times when in opposition; then they create hard times when they are in power. During last session I was very much interested in listening to the various members from the city of Toronto get up in this house and tell us of the terrible conditions existing in that city. I do not doubt but that some of them were wise enough to realize that- such conditions did not exist, but like the little birds in the nest they all held together for fear they would all fall out. When it comes to calamity howling, however, they have to yield the laurels to the hon. member for Hamilton, because I think he may be well dubbed the "Calamity Ann" of this house. However, after listening to all this talk of the terrible conditions in Toronto I had occasion to attend a banquet in that city, at which the mayor of Toronto said that his city was the most prosperous city not only in Canada but on the North American continent. That was enough to make me gasp with amazement, but the mayor elaborated the point, quoting all the building figures and telling of the preparations they were making to provide for a population of 1,000,000 happy people.

all they needed was protection. Many farmers believed them, with the result that the pool movement was a loss and one of the contributing factors to that loss was the argument advanced by my Conservative friends that a tariff was the only thing that would help those farmers.
I want to deal with the tariff on tobacco because the hon. member for South Essex stated that an increased tariff would mean an increased price to the grower in southern Ontario. A short time ago there was a hearing before the tariff board and experts in the tobacco industry gave evidence. This very question came up as to whether or not a tariff would be of any value to the tobacco grower in southern Ontario, and Mr. Richardson. speaking on behalf of the cigar manufacturers of Canada, said:
The issue having been raised that restoration of the 1913 2S cent leaf duties would seriously affect domestic production, we are prepared to prove that, on the contrary, it would actually benefit the grower of cigar leaf in Canada.
These men are all experts in their particular line; this question was carefully studied from all angles, and this is what they find: under the 28 cent tariff in 1919 the farmer was getting 25 cents a pound for his tobacco. The Conservatives increased' the tariff to 40 cents a pound, and would you believe it, the price actually dropped to 10i cents a pound to the farmer the following year, showing that the tobaccos that came into Canada at that time were not competitive tobaccos any more than they are to-day. The manufacturer has to import a certain amount of American tobacco, for he puts out a standardized product and he must maintain it. If a tariff did not help the farmers then, it could not help them now, and in my opinion it would injure them. I can understand the position of the manufacturer. If we further tax his raw material entering Canada that goes into the finished product, which sells at a price which does not vary, either he has to increase the price to the consumer or lower the price to the producer, and he is in a much better position to lower the price to the producer than to increase the price to the consumer.
In regard to the price of the finished product, I have a word of criticism against my hon. friend the Minister of Finance. There is only one way in which the government can help the tobacco industry in southern Ontario other than by following the trade policies now pursued, and that is to lower the excise tax on manufactured tobacco. This particular industry seems to be the subject of a very high tax. The excise tax in Canada is such that it just about equals the wholesale price in the

The Budget-Mr. Hepburn

United States, and when a Canadian visitor in the city of Detroit for example sees there two packages of tobacco selling for 25 cents while one package of the same brand sells for 25 cents in Canada, the temptation to smuggle is almost irresistible, and under the conditions I do not blame particularly the man who smuggles. I say that this extreme tax should not be maintained. In the hearing held before *the tariff board I was pleased to see that Mr. Darby of the Canadian Council of Agriculture in making his comments said:
Thanks to the returning prosperity and the general improvement of economic conditions, the national revenues are showing considerable buoyancy and several successive reductions of taxation have been possible. The prospect is that still further reductions in taxation will shortly be possible. In these circumstances, Mr. Chairman, the claims of the consumers of cigars and cigarettes to some alleviation of the taxes falling upon these commodities may properly be given careful consideration.
Another gentleman, Mr. Deaehman, the Secretary of the Consumers League, had this to say before the tariff board:
I support the application on the ground of its obvious reasonableness. There appears to be every evidence in what has been submitted that the taxation is now so high as to curtail the revenue, both by restricting consumption and by encouraging smuggling. I can see no reason why a tax which is so high as to defeat its purpose should be longer retained, and it seems to me this ease is so palpable as not to need further argument.
I have confidence enough in the Minister of Finance to feel, that when he brings down his next budget, which I hope will be another tax reducing budget, cognizance will be taken of this inequality and that equity will be done to all parts of Canada.
There is another matter which I want to bring to the attention of the house. Our friend from South Essex referred to the fact that he did not think there was unanimity of opinion on the government benches. I would like to counter by asking how much unanimity there is on the Conservative benches with regard to a speech made a few days ago by my good friend the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Smith). Speakmg on behalf of the province he represents, he was advocating an increased tariff on coal, and he said:
I know there are many difficulties in the way of the application of the tariff in its relation to the coal industry, but I am not by any means abandoning what I have always maintained to be one of the things necessary to help the industry, namely, a higher tariff on coal. I have heard the slur cast across the floor of the house many times, but I do not think there is any disagreement, so far as the members on this side of the house are concerned, with
[Mr. Hepburn.)
respect to properly and adequately protecting every legitimate industry in this Dominion. That has always been the stand of the Conservative party, and that policy has never been abandoned by that party so far as I am able to ascertain.
That is a very broad statement, and I watched with considerable interest to see how it would be received by members on the opposition benches. The applause was most enthusiastic. One would judge that they were sincere in leading the house and the country to believe that there was unanimity of opinion with regard to increasing the tariff on coal Coming from the province of Ontario, where we have to import our coal and use 13,000.000 tons per year, I would like to have something more definite in the way of a policy with regard to coal from the opposition members. I would like to ask if the policy enunciated by the hon. member for Cumberland is the policy of the great Conservative party, because we who have to import coal want to know it before the next general election. In the railway committee a year ago I opposed the idea of subsidizing Alberta coal. I said that the thing was not feasible, and that has since been proved to be the case. A tariff on coal would not have the effect of making the consumer in southern Ontario use a single ton more of Alberta or Nova Scotia coal. The only effect it would have would be to increase the cost to the consumer. I would like to ask the leader of the opposition what is his policy in that regard. I do not hope to get a definite answer because I recall an answer that he made some time ago. He had been complaining loud and long about the amount, of farm implements coming into this country. He did not believe in allowing farmers to buy their implements as cheaply as they could, and he said that the government had the tools in its hands to stop this importation. But when the Finance minister got up and asked him if he would stop it if he were in office by the application of a higher tariff, I was amazed at the dexterity by which the leader of the opposition evaded that, question. He said that he was too old a politician to be caught by such a question. I want to tell him that he is going to be caught by these two questions when he comes to southern Ontario, because we are going to know whether he is fooling us or whether he is fooling the people c.f Nova Scotia in regard to coal, and we are going to know as farmers what he is going to do about the tariff on agricultural implements.

The Minister of National Revenue will answer that.

The. Budget.-Mr. Irvine

In the few moments I have left, let me say that I am going to vote against the amendment of our Conservative friends with considerable gusto. It is just a foolish gesture intended to lead the farmers up a blind alley. I am happy to say that the Canadian farmer is the only farmer the world over who has not succumbed to the high tariff policies enunciated by so many Conservatives all over the world, policies which are restricting world trade. If any country in the world to-day needs wider markets, it is Canada, and if there is any country in the world where the policy of higher tariffs is not applicable to-day it is this Dominion.
With regard to the subamendment of the Progressives, I would like very much to support it because I believe in the principle of the British preference. I believe, further, that if by the proposed legislation of congress they make it. harder for us to sell the products of this country to the United States, we shall have to market our goods in other countries, and the great field ahead of us in that respect, I believe, is in developing further the British preference. But that is the policy of this government, and I cannot for one moment see the wisdom of nullifying all the good that has been done in bringing down this budget by voting for the subamendment, although I believe in it in principle. So I shall have to vote against it and support this government, believing that in doing so I am representing the sentiments of the people of the county of Elgin, which county has returned to the Liberal fold after being for thirty years under Conservative domination.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take a very few minutes of the time of the house to reply to the argument which was put forward to-night and especially directed against the amendment to the amendment by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). I do not know whether we should take the arguments on the budget, the amendment, and so forth, as seriously as some of us do, particularly after what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said to-day, that this is no place for an amendment, that the only thing an amendment can possibly mean is a vote of censure on the government. Then in reply to my question, what was the use of moving an amendment, the Prime Minister informed us that there was a place for such things. I have been a member of the house for five or six years, but I have never yet discovered that place. I suppose if we were to move an amendment to any single item of the budget
78594-91 i
when it reaches committee of the whole we would be met by precisely the same argument.
However, I wish to address myself in particular to the remarks of the hon. member for Labelle. The hon. gentleman is always interesting; at times he is refreshing. His erudition is unquestioned. I always admire his wide knowledge of affairs and his great ability in presenting his views to the house. However, the interpretation which he at times put upon certain facts of history might be very sharply questioned even by gentlemen who may be equally well informed. He attacks the amendment to the amendment on the ground that it favours a protective policy, and he proceeds to prove his case on this assumption. I must say that, considering all the speeches I have listened to from the hon. gentleman, he has made a poorer job at proving his case to-night than on any other occasion that I can recall. So far as I am aware, there is only one way in which an increase of the British preference can possibly be interpreted as protection, and to that way the hon. member did not direct his argument. If in our amendment to the amendment we were to ask that the tariff be increased against all other countries in order that the British preference might be correspondingly increased, then there would be grounds for the argument that it was a method of protection. But no such thing is advocated. Our amendment to the amendment suggests a reduction of the tariff against Great Britain in order that we may increase the preference. By what manner of means the hon. member for Labelle was able to satisfy himself that this meant increased protection, I cannot understand.
The hon. gentleman proceeded to tell us that he agreed with the policy as announced by the Prime Minister this afternoon. That policy, in a word, was that Canada was from now on to adjust her fiscal policy according to circumstances. That is a new policy for the Liberal party. I have no criticism of the policy; in fact I endorse it. It is the utterance of statesmanship. It makes due allowance for that great invisible government- circumstances-which more or less controls the activities of all governments. But I do want to say that the Liberal party never won an election on a platform of that kind, and I venture to say that they never will. But that was not the only policy announced today by the Prime Minister. In the platform of the Liberal party I find this policy:
That the British preference be increased to 50 per cent of the general tariff, and that the Liberal party hereby pledges itself to implement by legislation the provisions of thi' resolution when returned to power.
The Budget-Mr. Irvine

We have heard those things somewhere before. But the point is, if the hon. member for Labelle regards the preference amendment which we have moved as equivalent to protection, and for that reason cannot support it, I am at a loss to understand how he can support the policy of the Prime Minister when to increase the British preference to 50 per cent of the general tariff is the policy of the Liberal party, and was specifically referred to by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) as being the keystone. It is moved from 50 per cent of the general tariff to be the keystone; next they will have a chart, and after that a star. You know all great mariners guide their vessels by the stars of the heavens, but they never expect to lassoo those stars and pull them down to the deck where they can look at them. So the policy of the Liberal party is very much like the star that guides the mariner; they always leave it in the heavens to guide them because next year they might need it to bring them into the port of power.
But to return to the argument of the hon. member for Labelle. He was not at all convincing in stating that the increasing of the British preference by reduction of the British tariff could by any possible means be construed as a high tariff policy. In fact he said himself that such a policy would result in bringing into this country German goods, French goods, Belgian goods and goods from every European country, which would be shipped over here from Britain with the British stamp on them. That was his argument. Well, if the policy of preference is going to result in greater importations, is that the usual result of a protective policy? Surely he is lacking in logic there. The logic of the increase of the British preference would be this, that those countries outside the preference, if they desired to trade with Canada, would have to lower their tariffs; and in such circumstances I presume we would be prepared to lower our tariffs in so far as they are concerned, and thu3 make a step towards the great star which guides the Liberal party.
But the platform of the Liberal party as announced to-day by the Prime Minister is not only a new policy of shaping legislation according to circumstances, but it includes also, as I have pointed out, the preference policy of increasing the British preference to 50 per cent of the general tariff. The

Liberal party has been elected on that platform on three successive occasions. Now it appears that the Prime Minister is afraid to implement it for fear of what the United States may think or may do. But in any case I would defy the hon. member for Labelle to vote against our amendment to the amendment on the basis of the argument which he advances, and at the same time still hold to his view to vote for the policy of the present government.
Now, of course, I welcome the new policy of the Liberal party-if they will only adhere to it during the next election. But let them go to the west, for instance, and say: Now, Mr. Farmer, we don't know really what we will do if we are elected. We are going to fix up our next budget according to circumstances, and all the budgets of the next parliament will be so fixed. We don't know what the United States is going to do, we don't know what anybody is going to do; therefore we don't know what we are going to do. So if you elect us, what will happen? Why, we might have to raise our tariff in order to meet circumstances, or we might have to lower it, or leave it as it is, according as circumstances might dictate. That would be precisely what the government would do in so far as their action might ba concerned. But would they go to the people on that policy? I venture to say they would not. But to me the policy means to-day either that the carefully worded clauses in the budget-worded I presume by the Minister of Finance-are intended as a veiled threat of retaliation to the United States, or else that the government will wait until the American fiddle plays and then dance to its tune. It means one of these two things so far as I am able to interpret the Prime Minister's speech and the budget itself.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me ask the hon. member for Labelle-I hope he will read my speech to-morrow in Hansard, because I have no doubt he will make another speech on the amendment-let me ask him, I say, to tell me what he advises under the circumstances. He makes the charge that such a policy as we advocate in the amendment to the amendment involves certain sentiment, that it is not business, that it was fathered by sentiment; and he suggests that we throw all sentiment overboard so far as policy is concerned. I agree with him in that regard. But I was wondering whether there was not

a considerable amount of sentiment in his opposition to that subamendment. Are we the only people who are swayed by sentiment? Is the hon. member for Labelle absolutely void of it when he makes such a speech as he has made to-night against the amendment to the amendment? I do not wish to impute that to him, but at least it is suspicious; and if he is suspicious of our policy as being sentimental, we can at least return the possible suggestion of the same being the case with respect to himself. But let me assure the hon. gentleman that it is a matter of business with the western agriculturists; it is not a matter of sentiment. The western farmers have said again and again that they are not interested in the colour of the whiskers of any man with whom they do business; they do not care what part of the country he comes from or what country he lives in. They want to trade with him. That is not sentiment but business. But I want the hon. member for Labelle to tell us what we are going to do. The United States has shut us out of its market for farm produce. We do not wish to retaliate by asking this government to raise tariffs against that country. But at the same time we must find a market for our goods, and so we suggest that we lower the tariff to Great Britain, increasing their preference, and thereby probably finding a larger market for our produce. And it might be that such an action would have an effect upon the United States, in that if it desires to trade with Canada it might see fit not only to refrain from raising its tariff against us but to reduce it very materially. I hope therefore that if the hon. member for Labelle favours us to-morrow with another portion of his wisdom he will kindly go a little more into detail and prove not only to his own satisfaction but to the satisfaction of reasonable members of this house-and they would not be very many-that a reduction in the tariff to give a greater preference to Great Britain need not be construed as having no other meaning than an increase in tariffs.
